title: "Introduction"

## From Area-Level to Unit-Level

Unit-level small area estimation (SAE) is useful when individual or household survey records are available. Instead of modelling one summary estimate per area, unit-level models learn relationships in the survey microdata, then apply those relationships to a population dataset before aggregating predictions to areas.

| Approach | Model input | What gets modelled | How the area estimate is produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| Area-level | One direct estimate per area | Area-level estimates and sampling variances | Direct estimates are smoothed using area-level covariates, random effects, and optional spatial structure |
| Unit-level | Survey records | Individual or household outcomes | The model predicts outcomes for population units or cells, then aggregates predictions to areas |

## Unit-Level Estimation Workflow

Unit-level estimation usually has two linked steps:

1. **Multilevel regression:** Fit a model to the survey microdata. The model learns how individual traits, household traits, area covariates, and geographic random effects predict the outcome. A simple continuous-outcome version can be written as:
    $$
    y_{di} = x_{di}^{\top}\beta + u_d + e_{di},
    $$
    where $y_{di}$ is the outcome for unit $i$ in area $d$, $x_{di}$ contains unit-level predictors, and $u_d$ is an area effect.

2. **Poststratification:** Apply the fitted model to population cells, then aggregate the cell predictions to the small-area geography using the cell counts.

For this tutorial, the population auxiliary data are represented as cross-tabulated cells. This is the standard MRP setup and is usually more realistic than assuming a complete one-row-per-person population dataset is available.

| Input | Example | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Survey microdata | one row per survey respondent with `commute_distance`, MSOA, weights, and predictors | Fits the multilevel regression model |
| Population cells | one row per MSOA-by-predictor cell with `pop_count` | Provides the poststratification weights |

These workbooks demonstrate MRP using Bayesian statistics in R with `INLA`.
